204.title: A yellow leaf (235–238)
204.hook: you are now like a withered leaf; make yourself an island, work hard, be wise
204.howItsDone: Buddhists often reflect on death as a spur to practice, and the Buddha's advice to be an island to oneself is often quoted as a call to rely on one's own effort and the teaching.

segments.voice: Yesterday, dvāra: body, tongue and mind. Your line was the mind is where anger first knocks. Today, chapter eighteen begins: impurity.
screen: `THE MIND IS WHERE ANGER FIRST KNOCKS.`

segments.voice: Pick up a leaf in late autumn, one of the yellow ones that let go of the branch without any wind at all. It's light, dry and a little curled, and it still has every vein in place, like a map of a life. It was green in May. It didn't notice the change until it was nearly done. Most of us are the same: the years feel slow until one day they don't. Chapter eighteen of the Dhammapada opens by holding up a leaf like that and saying, gently but directly, this is you. Then it tells you what to build.
screen: `A LEAF IN LATE AUTUMN.` → `GREEN IN MAY.` → `THIS IS YOU.`

segments.voice: Verse two thirty-five, in Max Müller's translation: "Thou art now like a sear leaf, the messengers of death (Yama) have come near to thee; thou standest at the door of thy departure, and thou hast no provision for thy journey." Sear is an old word for dry and withered. The messengers of death, in the Pali, are Yama's men, death's own servants, already standing near. The picture is someone at the door, about to leave on a long trip, with no packed bag and no food for the road. The old commentary says these verses were spoken to an old man near the end of his life, as a gentle push to make good use of what remained. Then the answer, verse two thirty-six: "Make thyself an island, work hard, be wise!" In a flood, an island is the one piece of ground the water can't cover. The Pali word is dīpa, the word you met on day seventy-nine, when the Buddha, near the end, told Ānanda to be islands to themselves. Island or lamp, it can be read either way. What this verse adds is the building material: effort and wisdom, gathered while there's still time. None of this is meant to frighten anyone. The leaf is simply honest, and a leaf that knows it's a leaf can still do a great deal of good before it lets go.

segments.voice: If you have a leaf nearby, hold it; if not, picture one, yellow and light in your palm, and feel, without drama, that your time is not endless. Ask yourself what one thing that really matters you keep putting off, a conversation, a practice, a kindness, a letter, and let it come up on its own. Hold it next to the leaf, then let both rest, and sit on your island: this breath, this ground, steady in the flood.
Dīpa. Island, and also lamp: verse two thirty-six says make yourself an island, after verse two thirty-five calls you a withered leaf at the door of departure.
Your line: make an island. Effort and wisdom, while there's still time. See you tomorrow.

205.title: The smith and the silver (239–243)
205.hook: as a smith removes impurities from silver, little by little; ignorance the greatest taint
205.howItsDone: Buddhist practice is often described as gradual purification, and teachers use the smith and the silver to encourage steady daily effort rather than dramatic change.

segments.voice: Yesterday, dīpa: at the door of the journey, make yourself an island. Your line was make an island.

Take out an old silver spoon, the kind that sat in a drawer for years. It's gone dark, almost black in places. Rub it with a soft cloth and a little polish, and at first nothing happens. Then a faint gleam appears at the edge of the bowl. Rub more, and a little more of it comes back. You can't polish the whole spoon in one stroke. But stroke by stroke, the silver was there all along. Chapter eighteen of the Dhammapada puts a silversmith right in the middle of its teaching.
screen: `A TARNISHED SILVER SPOON.` → `A FAINT GLEAM AT THE EDGE.` → `THE SILVER WAS THERE ALL ALONG.`

segments.voice: Verse two thirty-nine, in Max Müller's translation: "Let a wise man blow off the impurities of his self, as a smith blows off the impurities of silver one by one, little by little, and from time to time." Picture an ancient smith at the furnace, melting silver and blowing the dross off the top, not all of it in one breath. The chapter's name is Malavagga, and mala means a stain, a taint, the dross. The old commentary tells of a brahmin who noticed monks' robes getting wet from dew as they walked through long grass, so he cleared the grass. Later he saw them getting dusty, so he spread sand. Then he built a shelter against the sun and rain. One small thing at a time, never a grand plan, and the Buddha praised him with this verse. Then the chapter lists taints, the way a household list would. Verse two forty-one: "The taint of prayers is non-repetition; the taint of houses, non-repair". A chant you stop reciting fades from memory. A house you stop mending falls apart. Neglect is its own kind of stain. Then the heaviest line, verse two forty-three: "But there is a taint worse than all taints,--ignorance is the greatest taint." Ignorance, avijjā, isn't about not knowing facts. It's not seeing how things really are: that they change, that craving hurts. The verse calls it worse than all the rest, and ends by telling the monks to throw it off. Which is why the polishing never stops. The silver is there.

segments.voice: If you can, pick up something small that needs care, a spoon, your glasses, a mug with a stain, or picture one, and slowly wipe it, just a little, noticing the small change. Then close your eyes and do the same with the mind: with each out-breath, let one small speck of irritation or worry blow off the top, like dross from silver. Not all of it; one by one, little by little.
Mala. A stain, a taint, the dross: verse two thirty-nine says as a smith blows the impurities off silver, one by one, little by little, the wise clear their own.
Your line: little by little. One by one, and from time to time. On we go.

206.title: Other people's faults (244–255)
206.hook: others' faults are easy to see, our own hard; we winnow theirs like chaff and hide our own (Dhammapada 252)
206.howItsDone: Buddhist monastics regularly confess their own faults to one another, and teachers often cite verse 252 to turn attention from criticizing others to examining oneself.

segments.voice: Yesterday, mala: dross blown off one by one, little by little. Your line was little by little.

Hand someone a stranger's essay and a red pen, and the mistakes leap off the page: a clumsy sentence here, a missing word there. Hand them their own essay, and the same mistakes go invisible. Or listen to a friend describe her sister, every flaw laid out in perfect detail. Ask for her own three biggest flaws, and there's a long pause. A perfect view of other people, and a blind spot the size of a truck about ourselves. Chapter eighteen names it exactly.
screen: `A RED PEN ON SOMEONE ELSE'S ESSAY.` → `ON YOUR OWN ESSAY, NOTHING.` → `A BLIND SPOT THE SIZE OF A TRUCK.`

segments.voice: Verse two fifty-two, in Max Müller's translation: "The fault of others is easily perceived, but that of oneself is difficult to perceive; a man winnows his neighbour's faults like chaff, but his own fault he hides, as a cheat hides the bad die from the gambler." Two pictures in one verse. First, winnowing: at harvest, farmers tossed grain into the wind so the light chaff would blow away. Picture someone tossing another person's faults high into the air, scattering them across the whole village. Second, a cheat at dice, hiding the bad die so no one notices it. That's what we do with our own. The Pali word for fault here is vajja, something to be avoided, something blameworthy. The next verse warns what happens to the fault-finder. Verse two fifty-three: "If a man looks after the faults of others, and is always inclined to be offended, his own passions will grow". The irony is sharp. Constant judging doesn't make you better. It feeds the very things you're judging. Just before these lines, verse two fifty-one gives four more pictures: "There is no fire like passion, there is no shark like hatred, there is no snare like folly, there is no torrent like greed." Then the chapter closes with a reminder that a person isn't made holy by outward show, which is where tomorrow's chapter picks up. None of this says other people have no faults. It says the eye that sees theirs so clearly would do its best work turned around.

segments.voice: Think of someone whose faults you know by heart, name one silently, and gently turn the same bright light around: is there any trace of it in you? Not to punish yourself, just to look, the way you'd check your own mirror; often there's a small echo, and if there isn't, look for the fault you'd least like anyone to see. When you've seen it, oh, there it is, set it down and let the breath be plain and open.

Your line: easy to see others. Hard to see ourselves. Day two hundred six, done.

207.title: Gray hair isn't wisdom (256–262)
207.hook: one is not learned because he talks much, nor an elder because his hair is gray
207.carry: wisdom can live in any body
207.howItsDone: In Theravada monasteries seniority is counted by rains retreats since ordination, and senior monks are called thera; these verses remind the community that the title means little without the qualities behind it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, vajja: others' faults winnowed like chaff, our own hidden like a bad die. Your line was easy to see others. Today, chapter nineteen begins: the just.

Every office has one: the person who talks the most in meetings, so everyone assumes they know the most. Every family has one too: the relative who reminds you they've been around longer, so they must be right. And sometimes it's the quiet twenty-five-year-old in the corner who actually understands the problem, or the grandmother who says almost nothing and sees everything. Loud isn't learned. Old isn't wise. Easy to say, and easy to forget in the moment. Chapter nineteen of the Dhammapada sorts the real thing from the look of it.
screen: `THE ONE WHO TALKS THE MOST.` → `THE ONE WHO'S BEEN AROUND LONGEST.` → `LOUD ISN'T LEARNED.`

segments.voice: The chapter is called Dhammaṭṭhavagga, the chapter of the one who stands in the dhamma, and it pulls apart labels and the qualities they're supposed to stand for. A judge isn't just because he forces a decision. Verse two fifty-eight, in Max Müller's words: "A man is not learned because he talks much; he who is patient, free from hatred and fear, he is called learned." Learning shows up as patience and fearlessness, not volume. Then verse two sixty: "A man is not an elder because his head is grey". The Pali word for elder is thera, the same word in Theravāda, the way of the elders. And the verse has a sharp name for someone merely old: moghajiṇṇa, in Müller's English, old-in-vain. Aged, but for nothing. So what makes a real elder? Verse two sixty-one: "He in whom there is truth, virtue, love, restraint, moderation, he who is free from impurity and is wise, he is called an elder." The commentary tells a story that turns it around. A group of monks came to visit the Buddha, and on their way in they passed a small, youthful-looking monk named Bhaddiya, who was just leaving. The Buddha asked if they'd seen the elder who had just gone out. They said they'd only seen a young novice. The Buddha told them the one they passed was an elder indeed, awakened. It wasn't his age that made him one. Wisdom can live in any body, at any age. So can its absence.
screen: `LABELS AND WHAT THEY STAND FOR.` · `LEARNED MEANS PATIENT, UNAFRAID.` · `THERA — AN ELDER, OR OLD-IN-VAIN.` · `THE SMALL MONK WAS THE ELDER.` · then, large: `GRAY HAIR ISN'T WISDOM.`

segments.voice: Think of one person who has really taught you something, not by talking a lot but by who they are, older or younger than you, and picture what they had: patience, honesty, restraint. If gratitude comes, let it stay a moment. Then ask quietly which of those qualities you could grow without announcing it, something to earn slowly, not claim, and let the question rest with the breath.
Thera. An elder: verse two sixty says one isn't an elder because the head is gray; truth, virtue, kindness and restraint make an elder.
Your line: wisdom can live in any body. Gray hair or not. See you tomorrow.

208.title: Not by shaving the head (263–272)
208.hook: a shaven head doesn't make a monk; the one who quiets evil is the true samana
208.howItsDone: Monks and nuns shave their heads and wear robes as signs of renunciation, and the tradition itself teaches, in verses like these, that the signs matter only when the practice behind them is real.

segments.voice: Yesterday, thera: not learned for talking much, not an elder for a gray head. Your line was wisdom can live in any body.

You can buy the running shoes, the fitness watch and the matching outfit, and post a photo at the start of the trail. None of it runs a single mile. You can set a meditation cushion in the corner of your bedroom, beautifully lit, with a candle and a small statue. The cushion doesn't sit. Owning the gear is one thing and doing the work is another, and the gear is always easier. Even in the Buddha's day, people noticed that robes and a shaved head could be worn by anyone. Chapter nineteen goes on to test the titles of the holy life.
screen: `THE SHOES DON'T RUN.` → `THE CUSHION DOESN'T SIT.` → `THE LOOK IS ALWAYS EASIER.`

segments.voice: Verse two sixty-four, in Max Müller's translation: "Not by tonsure does an undisciplined man who speaks falsehood become a Samana". A samaṇa was a wandering renunciant, one who had left home for the spiritual life. Then the verse plays with the word. Two sixty-five: "He who always quiets the evil, whether small or large, he is called a Samana (a quiet man), because he has quieted all evil." In Pali, samaṇa sounds like the verb for calming, quieting. So the real samaṇa is the one who has quieted harm, not the one with the haircut. The chapter does this again and again. A bhikkhu, a monk, isn't one just because he asks for alms. A muni, a sage, isn't one just because he keeps silent, from mona, silence; a true sage weighs things well: "he who in this world weighs both sides is called a Muni." An ariya, a noble one, isn't one if he harms living beings; he's called noble "because he has pity on all living creatures". Every title gets turned back to what it's supposed to mean. Then the chapter warns even the sincere. Vows, learning, deep meditation, solitude: none of it is a reason to relax. "Bhikshu, be not confident as long as thou hast not attained the extinction of desires." This isn't a dig at monks; monks and nuns themselves chant these verses. It's a mirror for anyone with a label: Buddhist, meditator, good person. The practice makes it. The label never does.

segments.voice: For these two minutes there's no audience at all: no photo, no streak, no label, just the breath coming in and going out. If a thought shows up, I'm good at this, or I'm bad at this, notice that it's another label, and let it go. Quiet one small agitation, then the next; that's all a samaṇa does.

209.title: They only point (273–276)
209.hook: of paths the eightfold is best; you yourself must make the effort; the Buddhas only show the way
209.howItsDone: Buddhists revere the Buddha as the teacher who found and showed the path, while holding that each person must walk it through their own effort; the eightfold path and four noble truths are taught across Buddhist schools.

segments.voice: Yesterday, not by shaving the head: the true samaṇa is the one who has quieted harm. Your line was the practice makes it. Today, chapter twenty begins: the way.

You're lost in a strange city, and you ask someone for directions. They're wonderful. They draw a little map on a napkin, name the landmarks, even walk you to the corner and point: three blocks that way, then left at the bakery. Then they go back to their day, because that's all anyone can do. They can't walk the three blocks for you. Stand on the corner admiring the napkin, and you'll never get there. Chapter twenty of the Dhammapada is called the way, and one of its verses says, very plainly, what even a Buddha can and can't do.
screen: `DIRECTIONS ON A NAPKIN.` → `THREE BLOCKS, THEN LEFT.` → `THEY CAN'T WALK IT FOR YOU.`

segments.voice: The chapter opens with a list of bests. Verse two seventy-three, in Max Müller's translation: "The best of ways is the eightfold; the best of truths the four words; the best of virtues passionlessness; the best of men he who has eyes to see." The eightfold way is the path this course has met before: right view, intention, speech, action, livelihood, effort, mindfulness and concentration. The four words are the four noble truths. Then, after urging the listener onto the way, comes verse two seventy-six, the heart of today: "You yourself must make an effort. The Tathagatas (Buddhas) are only preachers." Tathāgata is one of the Buddha's own titles, the thus-gone one. The Pali for only preachers is akkhātāro: the ones who tell, who declare, who point out. The verse never promises that the Tathagatas walk the way for anyone. The Buddha, in this verse, is the person on the corner pointing down the street. The walking is yours. The Pali word for effort here is ātappa, from a root meaning heat: the warmth of steady, ardent work. Later Buddhist traditions, especially Chan and Zen, loved a related image: the teaching is a finger pointing at the moon. Don't stare at the finger. And in an early discourse, the Buddha compares the teaching to a raft, for crossing a river, not for carrying on your head once you're across. The images differ, but the point is the same: a teacher shows the way. Your feet make the journey.

segments.voice: Picture whatever is pointing for you, a teacher, a verse, even this lesson, and notice where it points: toward this breath, this body, this moment. Then take one step: put your whole attention on a single breath, from its first cool edge in the nostrils to the last of the out-breath, and then another. Nobody else can take it for you, and nobody needs to.

Your line: your feet make the journey. Directions are not the walk itself. Until tomorrow.

210.title: All created things (277–279)
210.hook: all created things pass, all are painful, all forms are without self; seeing this, one turns from suffering
210.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers across schools teach the three marks of existence, impermanence, unsatisfactoriness and not-self, and meditators often use verses 277–279 as reflections to return to.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Tathāgata: you yourself must make the effort; the Buddhas show the way. Your line was your feet make the journey. Today, the end of the week.

Look around the room you're in. The coffee going cold. The phone battery a little lower than an hour ago. The light through the window at a different angle than this morning. The plant that has grown a leaf you haven't noticed. Your own body, a few more cells replaced since you woke up. Nothing in the room is holding still. Not one thing. Everyone knows this, and still plans as if the world were a photograph. Chapter twenty holds three short verses, all built alike, that say so.
screen: `THE COFFEE GOING COLD.` → `NOTHING IN THE ROOM HOLDS STILL.` → `THREE SHORT VERSES.`

segments.voice: The three verses share one shape. Each names something true of everything, then says the one who knows and sees it grows weary of suffering and turns from it: "this is the way to purity." Verse two seventy-seven, in Max Müller's words: "All created things perish". In Pali, sabbe saṅkhārā aniccā. Saṅkhārā means things that are put together, made of parts and causes. Anicca means impermanent: they don't last. Verse two seventy-eight: "All created things are grief and pain". Sabbe saṅkhārā dukkhā. Not that everything is miserable, but that nothing put together can give lasting satisfaction, because it's always slipping away. And verse two seventy-nine, in Müller's older English: "All forms are unreal". The Pali is sabbe dhammā anattā: all things are not-self. Nothing, anywhere, is a fixed, permanent self to hold onto. Buddhists call these the three marks of existence: impermanence, unsatisfactoriness, not-self. One small detail repays a close look. The first two verses say all saṅkhārā, all made things. The third says all dhammā, all things whatsoever, a wider word, so that even nibbāna, which isn't made, is included in not-self. And the Buddha's last words, in the long account of his final days, echo the first verse: all made things are subject to decay; strive on with diligence. It ends a week that kept pointing here. Make an island. Little by little. Easy to see others. Wisdom can live in any body. The practice makes it. Your feet make the journey. And today: all things pass.
screen: `SABBE SAṄKHĀRĀ ANICCĀ.` · `NOTHING MADE GIVES LASTING EASE.` · `SABBE DHAMMĀ ANATTĀ.` · `THE BUDDHA'S LAST WORDS.` · then, large: `ALL THINGS PASS.`

segments.voice: Watch three things change: the breath, each one beginning and ending, no two the same; a sound, a car, a bird, a hum, arriving and fading; a thought, appearing, staying a moment, and dissolving on its own. You don't have to make them pass; they already do. Just see it, and let the seeing be gentle.
All created things. Verses two seventy-seven to two seventy-nine: all made things pass, all are unsatisfying, all things are not-self; seeing this is the way to purity.
Your line: all things pass. The good and the hard alike. That's a week, and day two hundred ten.

original.note: Pali: something put together, a conditioned thing — sabbe saṅkhārā aniccā, all made things pass.

trapdoor: what you thought: everything dies, so why bother?

what a scholar hears: verses 277–278 say sabbe saṅkhārā, but 279 says sabbe dhammā, a wider term that includes the unconditioned; Müller's 'unreal' is an older rendering of anattā.
